turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, sit him up there. What's the problem today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's his skin, doctor. The backs of the knees and the elbows, dry and itchy, and he's scratching the life out of himself at night.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah the itchy bits. They go all scratchy and I can't leave them, it feels like little ants walking under the skin when the light goes off, and I scratch and scratch even when mam says stop.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long is this spell?
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sure he's had the dry skin since he was a baby. This bad bit is about six weeks. Umm, maybe a bit more.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waking with it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah. He wakes himself scratching. The sheets are a state in the morning.

[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): And then in the morning I feel like a wet rag, all floppy and heavy, because I was scratching all night and I didn't really sleep, and school is hard when I'm sleepy, but the itchy bits are why we came, not the school, the school is grand mostly.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any oozing? Yellow crusts?
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No crusts. Just dry and red.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. He's grand in himself, apart from the itch.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wheeze? Any trouble with the breathing?
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, not a bother with the breathing. Himself, his dad, has the asthma. Finn doesn't.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tummy pain? Runny eyes?

[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. My tummy is fine, I had porridge and it was grand. I can't hear myself think when the telly is loud in the kitchen but that's just the telly, not a sore thing. And my eyes don't run, they just blink normal.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What creams are on him?
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A grand big white tub, no smell on it, the label's worn off so I couldn't tell you the name. And a little pink tube for the sore patches.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Name or strength on the pink one?
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I don't know it. The chemist just said use the pink one. We put it on the elbows and the backs of the knees.

[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): The white one is cold, I do it myself sometimes, two squirts, and I rub and rub till it's all gone in, and the pink one is only a tiny dot, mam does that because she says I've overdone it if I squeeze too much out.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often, the white tub?
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most days. Well, when I remember. Some mornings we're out the door and it doesn't get done.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the pink tube?
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The pink tube, once a night on the patches, these last few weeks. Not every single night, if I'm honest.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything by mouth for the itch?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We had cetirizene. I think it was 10 mg, no, he's small, it was the 5 mg, one at night. I stopped it in March. It made him dopey for school.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you were given and didn't use?
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, they gave us fucidin last winter for a spot on his chin and I never opened it. Never gave it to him.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies? Medicines or creams?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing that I know of.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Elbows up. Let me see.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dry thickened patches, both elbow creases and the backs of both knees. No ooze. Skin's not hot. No infection that I can see.

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): They look like maps, all pinky and wrinkly, and when you press them it doesn't really hurt, it just itches after, like the ants come straight back, and the left knee is the worse one I think, or maybe the right, I forget which I scratch more.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is his eczema flaring. I'm changing the steroid.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the pink tube. I'll give you clobetasone, 0.05 percent, a thin layer twice a day on the patches only, for seven days, then stop it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a day, seven days, then stop. Grand.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep a plain moisturiser, lots of it, all over, three or four times a day. The white tub is fine if it's a plain one. Steroid on first, wait twenty minutes, then the moisturiser.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No soap in the bath. Nails short. Cotton at night.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. No soap, short nails, cotton.

[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Can I still have the blue bubbles? I like a big pile of them and then my skin goes all tight after, and mam says that's why the patches get cross with me, but the bubbles are the best bit of the bath.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No bubbles. They dry the skin.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll live. And if the seven days doesn't clear it?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it's not settling, or if it starts to weep, we might swab it then. Not today.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see him back in three weeks anyway.
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks. Do I book that at the desk?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Reception will put the three weeks in. If it weeps before that, ring us.

[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Will the ants go if I do the new cream and I don't scratch, because I try not to but then I forget and I do it in my sleep and I wake up and the skin is sore from me, and I don't mean to, it just happens.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): The itch should ease. Hands off it if you can.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks, doctor. Seven days of the new one, the white tub, and back in three weeks.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Off you go.

spec.situation: Mother brings a child with itchy dry patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, scratching; creams named by colour; father has asthma; doctor adjusts steroid cream and moisturiser advice.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

bad.reason: Use and frequency supported, but status wrong: pink tube was current until doctor said stop today.
bad.text: pink tube (frequency=once a night, duration=a few weeks, indication=patches, status=discontinued, reported_by=family_member)

omissions.text: Current rash described as dry and red; no crusts, just dry and red.
Sleep disturbance is causing daytime sleepiness and school is hard when sleepy.
Cetirizine was stopped in March because it made him dopey for school.
Fucidin had previously been given last winter for a spot on his chin but was never opened/never used.
Clobetasone 0.05% should be applied as a thin layer on the patches only, then stopped after seven days.
If the rash is not settling or if it starts to weep, then a swab may be taken; not doing a swab today.

The previous cetirizine was stopped because it made him dopey/sedated for school.
